title: Kedoshim: as yourself (Leviticus 19:18)
hook: "thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself"; Rabbi Akiva called it the great principle of the Torah

segments.voice: Yesterday in Kedoshim, a verse that won't let us just watch. Your line was don't stand idly by. Did you step in somewhere? Today, two verses later, a line that has traveled far beyond the chapter. Day four hundred fourteen.

This line turns up on posters, at weddings, in speeches, on bumper stickers. Words that familiar can slide right off. But it's only the second half of a verse. The first half rarely makes it onto the poster, and it changes how the famous part sounds. It's not about warm feelings for nice people. It's about the person who did harm last month, and the grudge that's been quietly kept ever since.
screen: `ON POSTERS AND BUMPER STICKERS.` → `THE HALF THAT COMES FIRST.` → `THE ONE WHO WRONGED YOU.`

segments.voice: First, the whole verse. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Thou shalt not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." The love comes right after the grudge. It's the alternative to revenge. Second, the knife. The Jerusalem Talmud explains vengeance with a picture. Someone is cutting meat, and the knife slips and cuts their hand. Would the cut hand turn around and stab the hand that held the knife? Of course not. They're one body. So, too, the people: hurting each other back is like a body attacking itself. Third, Rabbi Akiva. He called this verse a great principle of the Torah, klal gadol. His colleague Ben Azzai named a different verse as greater still: the line in Genesis about the generations of Adam, the human being made in God's likeness. Love your neighbor might depend on how you feel about yourself, some explain. Ben Azzai's verse grounds it in every person's dignity. The two teachings sit side by side in the sources. Fourth, how it's lived. When a man asked Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while standing on one foot, Hillel said: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Now go and learn. As yourself: a measure every person carries.
screen: `NO VENGEANCE, NO GRUDGE.` · `ONE BODY: THE CUT HAND.` · `AKIVA: THE GREAT PRINCIPLE.` · `HILLEL ON ONE FOOT.` · then, large: `AS YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one loving thing for a neighbor. Settle, and breathe. Think of a neighbor, literal or not: the person next door, at the next desk, in the next seat. Maybe even one you've got a small grudge against. Ask what you'd want if you were them today. A hand with groceries, a kind word, a returned favor, an apology accepted. Choose one thing, and picture doing it. The bell holds the time.
Kedoshim. The portion with love thy neighbor as thyself, which Rabbi Akiva called the great principle of the Torah, set right after the ban on grudges.
Your line: as yourself. Today, before you act toward someone, ask what you'd want in their place, and do that. Day four hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Some prayer books open the morning service with a line taking on the commandment of loving one's neighbor as oneself, a custom traced to the kabbalist Isaac Luria, and Hillel's summary is often taught in Jewish schools.

original.note: Hebrew: "and you shall love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18).

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to people.
what it means: instead of revenge or a grudge, treat others the way you'd want to be treated.
what a scholar hears: Akiva's klal gadol and Ben Azzai's reply are in the Sifra and the Jerusalem Talmud (Nedarim 9:4), which also gives the parable of the cut hand.

notes: Audit (10% sample): removed the unsourced claim that 'most people who quote it have never seen' the first half; hook head 'the half nobody quotes' now 'the half that comes first'.
JPS 1917 Lev 19:18 quoted in full from memory; confirm.
The knife/cut-hand parable is in the Jerusalem Talmud, Nedarim 9:4; confirm.

Akiva's klal gadol and Ben Azzai's Gen 5:1: Sifra Kedoshim 4:12 and Yerushalmi Nedarim 9:4; the explanation that Ben Azzai grounds it in dignity is a common reading (Bereshit Rabbah 24:7 adds Tanhuma's comment); confirm wording.
Luria's custom of accepting love of neighbor before prayer (cited in many siddurim): confirm.
